intro.text: After the user approves (or declines) consent at the LFI, the Authorization Server redirects them back to your registered redirect_uri. How you handle this callback is security-critical — mistakes here can allow CSRF attacks, token theft, and authorization code replay.

sections.heading: What the Authorization Server sends back

blocks.text: The callback URL will be of the form:

rows: The authorization code to exchange at /token. Single-use and short-lived
The value you sent in the Request JWT — must match what you stored before redirecting
The issuer of the Authorization Server that issued the code

sections.heading: Always confirm the state value matches

blocks.text: Confirm that the state value returned in the callback matches the one you set in your Request JWT. This protects against CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) attacks where a malicious page triggers an unintended authorization.

sections.heading: Confirm the response came from the expected Authorization Server

blocks.text: Check that the iss parameter matches the Authorization Server you sent the /par request to. This ensures the response comes from the expected LFI and not a confused deputy or misconfigured redirect.

sections.heading: Authorization codes are single-use and short-lived

blocks.text: Authorization codes are single-use and short-lived — typically valid for only a few minutes. Exchange the code immediately upon receipt.

items: Exchange the code at /token within seconds of receiving it — do not queue or defer
Do not accept callbacks that arrive long after the authorization request was initiated
Once a code has been exchanged successfully, treat it as consumed and reject any attempt to use it again

blocks.text: Store a timestamp when you send the user to /par. In your callback handler, reject any callback where too much time has elapsed since that timestamp (e.g. more than 10 minutes), even if state is otherwise valid.

sections.heading: Do only what's required, then redirect

blocks.text: When handling the callback, execute only the minimum necessary logic:

items: Exchange the code for tokens at /token
Redirect the user to the next step in your application flow

blocks.text: Avoid running complex business logic, sending external requests (other than /token ), or initiating sensitive operations at this stage. A failed or slow callback should not leave the user in an inconsistent state.
If validation fails or the code exchange returns an error, show the user a clean error message and discard all parameters from the callback. Do not log authorization codes or tokens.

sections.heading: The token response carries the current consent state

blocks.text: On a successful POST /token (HTTP 200), the Authorization Server returns not only the access_token and refresh_token but also the Consent object, including its current Status. See the token endpoint reference for details: CreateAccessTokenRequestV21 (OpenAPI: docs/public/openapi/v2.1/standards/uae-authorization-endpoints-openapi.yaml, schema AEAuthorizationEndpointsV21.AEAuthorizationCodeGrantTokenResponseProperties ).
Because access to resources requires both a valid access token and an authorized consent, the TPP can determine from this response whether resource access is permitted.

In most flows the consent status will be Authorized. However, for payment (Bank Service Initiation) consents that support and require multi-authorization, the consent status may instead be AwaitingAuthorization, indicating the first authorizer has approved but additional authorizers are still required before a payment can be made.
